FxHash/rustc-hash is the clearest real-world example of the non-cryptographic tier's assumption: its own README states explicitly that it gives up DoS resistance because the compiler's inputs aren't adversarial.

items.item: Rust's std HashMap chooses a keyed, randomly-seeded hash (SipHash 1-3) specifically for HashDoS resistance, with the speed trade-off against small/large keys stated in its own docs.

at.step: A real standard library's own choice

items.item: A HashMap built with a fixed (non-random) hasher in a const/static context loses HashDoS resistance entirely, per Rust's own docs' explicit warning.

at.step: A real standard library's own choice

items.item: SipHash is formally a PRF (pseudorandom function) — indistinguishable from a uniform random function — which is the actual property hash-flooding resistance needs, not merely "has a secret key."

at.step: A real pseudorandom function, not just a secret

items.item: The real correction: a merely randomly-seeded linear public hash family is still breakable by an attacker with timing/adaptive query access, via Gaussian elimination against the linear structure — the actual reason SipHash's PRF strength matters over naive random seeding alone.

at.step: What a random seed actually buys you

items.item: Hash flooding's documented history: the 1999 dnscache source-code comment, Crosby & Wallach's 2003 "algorithmic complexity attacks" paper (USENIX Security), and Klink & Wälde's December 2011 CCC 28c3 disclosure with a concrete real-world figure.

at.step: The attack this fast hash never promised to survive

items.item: The concrete mechanism of a collision-flooding attack: an attacker finds many inputs that hash to the same table index (a multicollision), degrading a hash table's expected O(1) per-operation cost to O(n).

at.step: The attack this fast hash never promised to survive

items.item: Cryptographic hashes (SHA-256, BLAKE3) are a third, slower-but-strongly-collision-resistant tier; BLAKE3 is itself faster than SHA-2 by design, but still far slower than XXH3 for the ordinary, non-adversarial case.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: SipHash was explicitly designed to be competitive in speed with popular non-cryptographic hash functions for short inputs, despite being a MAC-strength PRF — the reason it's usable as a general-purpose default hasher rather than too slow to ship.

at.step: A real pseudorandom function, not just a secret

items.item: Measured directly on the authoring machine, the fast tier (zlib.crc32) and the keyed/PRF tier (CPython's own hash()) run close together, empirically supporting the paper's own "competitive in speed" claim, while the cryptographic tier (SHA-256) is clearly and consistently ~8-9x slower.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: How a hash table actually resolves two keys that hash to the same slot (chaining, open addressing, SIMD group probing) is a separate concern from which hash function feeds it, and is this chapter's own next three topics, not this one's subject.

Universal hashing's formal guarantee (a provable bound on collision probability for any fixed input distribution, independent of what an adversary chooses) is the deeper theoretical tool that would fully justify "why keying helps" beyond this topic's empirical framing — out of scope because the syllabus itself skips "Universal and k-independent hashing" in this chapter.
